items.headline: Test landing pages by asking readers to explain them back
items.background: Landing page copy is notoriously hard to evaluate internally because authors are too close to the product to judge clarity. Most feedback methods ask for opinions rather than testing actual comprehension.
keyFindings: Ask new readers to describe what the product does, who it's for, and what happens after the CTA — before asking for opinions
Mismatches between intended and perceived purpose reveal messaging failures that aesthetic feedback misses
This method surfaces ambiguity in value propositions that founders and designers routinely overlook
items.implications: This technique is low-cost and applicable before any formal usability testing — useful for early-stage products or redesigns. If readers can't accurately describe the product unprompted, the copy needs work regardless of how good it looks.

items.headline: Utility-first features are the hardest to design well
items.background: Product teams often prioritize flashy, shareable features over the unglamorous functional ones users depend on daily. This piece uses a meal planning app's ingredient list as a case study in designing for silent, high-stakes utility.
keyFindings: Users never talk about functional features like grocery lists — but abandonment spikes when they fail
Precise formatting details like units, quantities, and ingredient grouping carry disproportionate usability weight
The absence of complaints about utility features is not evidence they're working — it's a measurement gap
items.implications: If you're building productivity or planning tools, invest QA and design attention in the mundane data-entry and output features, not just the ones that demo well. Silence from users about a feature is not the same as satisfaction.

items.headline: Nigerian VC pushes for mandatory AI literacy in schools
items.background: Debates over how early and formally AI and digital skills should be taught are intensifying globally, with industry voices increasingly pressuring governments to embed them in national curricula.
keyFindings: A Nigerian venture capitalist has formally urged the federal government to make AI and digital literacy compulsory subjects in schools
The call reflects growing concern that Nigeria's workforce pipeline is underprepared for AI-integrated industries
No specific curriculum framework or timeline was outlined in the reported recommendation
items.implications: Relevant for those working on edtech products or designing onboarding for non-technical users in emerging markets — baseline digital literacy cannot be assumed and is a live policy issue, not a solved one.
